# draw.io

> draw.io is free diagramming software, used since 2005, for flowcharts, UML, ER, network, cloud architecture and many other diagram types. It runs in the browser at app.diagrams.net, as a desktop app, and inside Google Drive, Docs and Slides, Microsoft SharePoint, OneDrive and Teams, Confluence, Jira, GitHub, VS Code and Notion. The editor source code is Apache 2.0 licensed, and diagrams are stored on your device or in the storage you choose, not on draw.io's servers.

This site (www.drawio.com) has the user documentation, the technical reference and the blog. Diagrams are saved as `.drawio` files, which contain mxGraph XML (see "The .drawio file format" below). AI assistants can create draw.io diagrams through the draw.io MCP server and plugins, from draw.io XML, Mermaid, PlantUML or CSV, and quick flowcharts from a list of their steps (the fast mode); see the "AI assistants (MCP)" section below.

To draw a diagram from Mermaid, PlantUML or CSV, call the tool create_diagram on the draw.io MCP server (https://mcp.draw.io/mcp) with the source text in one argument: mermaid, plantuml or csv. You don't place every shape in XML. The server converts the source into native draw.io shapes that stay editable, lays them out, styles them and returns the draw.io XML, with an app.diagrams.net link for clients that don't show the diagram. It converts Mermaid flowcharts, ER and sequence diagrams, PlantUML sequence and activity diagrams, and draw.io CSV. A syntax error comes back with its line and how to fix it. Other types, such as Mermaid gantt or PlantUML class diagrams, are converted by draw.io in the chat viewer.

Mermaid, sent as {"mermaid": "<the text>"}:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Order received] --> B{Paid?}
  B -->|yes| C[Ship order]
  B -->|no| D[Send reminder]
```

PlantUML, sent as {"plantuml": "<the text>"}, from @startuml to @enduml:

```plantuml
@startuml
Customer -> Shop: Place order
Shop --> Customer: Confirmation
@enduml
```

CSV in draw.io's CSV import format, sent as {"csv": "<the text>"}: the # lines set the label, the connections and the layout, then a header and one row per shape:

```csv
# label: %name%
# connect: {"from": "manager", "to": "name", "invert": true}
# layout: verticaltree
name,manager
CEO,
CTO,CEO
CFO,CEO
```

## Documentation

- [Documentation home](https://www.drawio.com/docs/): Overview of the draw.io documentation
- [About draw.io](https://www.drawio.com/docs/about/): The company, licence and privacy principles
- [Features](https://www.drawio.com/docs/features/): One-page overview of the application's features
- [Getting started](https://www.drawio.com/docs/getting-started/): Introduction to the draw.io diagram editor for new users
- [Using draw.io](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/): The user manual: shapes, connectors, styles, layers, export, import and more
- [Types of diagrams](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/): How to draw specific diagram types, including UML
- [Tutorials](https://www.drawio.com/docs/tutorials/): Step-by-step guides for specific features
- [Diagramming best practices](https://www.drawio.com/docs/best-practice/): General advice for clear diagrams
- [Technical reference](https://www.drawio.com/docs/reference/): Reference for developers, such as the .drawio file format, embed mode, plugins and keyboard shortcuts
- [Troubleshooting](https://www.drawio.com/docs/troubleshooting/): Solutions to common problems

## The .drawio file format

- [The .drawio file format](https://www.drawio.com/docs/reference/file-format/): The XML of .drawio files (mxfile, diagram, mxGraphModel, mxCell, mxGeometry, UserObject and styles), a minimal example, the compressed form, diagrams in .drawio.svg and .drawio.png images, and example files with their licences
- [mxfile.xsd](https://www.drawio.com/mxfile.xsd): XML Schema for the plain form of .drawio files, newest version. Version 1.0, which doesn't change: https://www.drawio.com/xsd/mxfile-1.0.xsd
- [Example diagrams](https://github.com/jgraph/drawio-diagrams): Example .drawio files and templates on GitHub, Apache License 2.0

## Generate diagrams with AI

- [Generate diagrams in draw.io](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/generate/): Use the Generate dialog in the editor to create a diagram from a text prompt
- [About the AI models and LLMs](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/generate/ai-models/): How diagram generation works, which models are used and what data is shared
- [Examples of generated diagrams](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/generate/generated-diagrams-examples/): Prompts and the diagrams they generated
- [Write better queries for AI generated diagrams](https://www.drawio.com/docs/best-practice/write-query-generate-diagram/): Prompting advice
- [Disable diagram generation](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/generate/generated-diagram-disable/): Turn the AI features off
- [Generate and validate draw.io diagrams with AI](https://www.drawio.com/docs/reference/diagram-generation/): Technical reference for generating draw.io XML with an LLM
- [Style reference for AI diagram generation](https://www.drawio.com/docs/reference/diagram-generation/style-reference/): Style keys and values for generated draw.io XML
- [Customise LLM backends](https://www.drawio.com/docs/reference/diagram-generation/configure-ai-options/): Configure the AI models and endpoints of the Generate dialog
- [Mermaid diagrams](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/mermaid/): Insert and edit Mermaid diagrams in draw.io

## AI assistants (MCP)

- [draw.io for AI assistants](https://www.drawio.com/mcp/): Overview, setup for Claude, Claude Code, ChatGPT, Codex, GitHub Copilot, Cursor and Antigravity, examples with prompts
- [Send Mermaid, PlantUML or CSV, get a draw.io diagram](https://www.drawio.com/docs/reference/diagram-generation/): The create_diagram arguments mermaid (28 diagram types), plantuml and csv, which types the server converts into editable draw.io shapes, and which go to the chat viewer
- [draw.io MCP server and plugins](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/generate/drawio-mcp-server/): The ways to use draw.io in AI assistants (MCP App Server, plugins, MCP Tool Server, self-hosting, project instructions), the formats the assistant writes in each, and the output formats
- [MCP tools and input formats](https://www.drawio.com/docs/reference/diagram-generation/): The hosted MCP App Server (https://mcp.draw.io/mcp) takes draw.io XML, Mermaid, PlantUML or CSV in create_diagram, and a description of a flowchart or swimlane diagram in create_semantic_diagram, the fast mode. The MCP Tool Server (npx @drawio/mcp) opens draw.io XML, Mermaid and CSV in the draw.io editor
- [Fast mode for quick flowcharts](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/generate/ai-assistants/prompts/): When the user asks for a quick, rough or cheap flowchart or swimlane diagram, the model calls create_semantic_diagram with the steps, lanes, transitions and a row and column per step, and the server lays out the diagram and routes the lines: 3 to 4 times faster, with less than half the output tokens. Flowcharts without lanes up to 24 steps, lane diagrams without a limit, calm colours only
- [Fast mode reference](https://github.com/jgraph/drawio-mcp/blob/main/shared/semantic/FAST-MODE.md): When models take create_semantic_diagram, its limits and the measurement; the description format is in https://github.com/jgraph/drawio-mcp/blob/main/shared/semantic/FORMAT.md
- [Use the diagram viewer in the chat](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/generate/ai-assistants/diagram-viewer/): Pan, zoom and open the diagrams an assistant shows in the chat
- [Write prompts for diagrams in AI assistants](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/generate/ai-assistants/prompts/): Mermaid or draw.io XML, quick diagrams, models, how to write the prompt
- [Diagram types and examples](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/generate/ai-assistants/diagram-types/): Example prompts and the diagrams they produced, and all supported diagram types
- [Change and style a diagram](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/generate/ai-assistants/edit-and-style/): Changes by prompt, colour themes and styles
- [Gallery](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/generate/ai-assistants/gallery/): An example of every diagram type with its prompt
- [Privacy policy for draw.io in AI assistants](https://www.drawio.com/trust/privacy-ai-assistants/): What the hosted MCP server at https://mcp.draw.io/mcp receives, uses and keeps
- [drawio-mcp on GitHub](https://github.com/jgraph/drawio-mcp): Source code and setup documentation of the MCP servers and plugins

## Integrations

- [Integrations overview](https://www.drawio.com/docs/integrations/): All platforms draw.io works with
- [Google](https://www.drawio.com/docs/integrations/google/): Google Drive, Docs, Sheets and Slides
- [Microsoft](https://www.drawio.com/docs/integrations/microsoft/): SharePoint, OneDrive and Teams
- [Atlassian](https://www.drawio.com/docs/integrations/atlassian/): Confluence and Jira
- [GitHub](https://www.drawio.com/docs/integrations/github/): Diagrams in GitHub repositories and Markdown
- [VS Code](https://www.drawio.com/docs/integrations/embed-diagrams-vscode/): Create diagrams directly in VS Code
- [Notion](https://www.drawio.com/docs/integrations/notion/): Store draw.io diagrams in Notion
- [Embed mode](https://www.drawio.com/docs/reference/embed-mode/): Embed the draw.io editor in your own application
- [Encode a diagram in a URL](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/export/export-to-url/): Open a diagram from a link

## Security and privacy

- [Security and privacy](https://www.drawio.com/docs/security/): How draw.io keeps diagram data secure and private
- [Privacy policy](https://www.drawio.com/trust/): The draw.io privacy policy and trust pages

## Optional

- [Full documentation in one file](https://www.drawio.com/llms-full.txt): Every documentation page as Markdown
- [Blog](https://www.drawio.com/blog/): Feature announcements and updates
- [Support](https://www.drawio.com/support/): How to get help
- [draw.io source code](https://github.com/jgraph/drawio): The draw.io editor on GitHub
- [draw.io editor](https://app.diagrams.net): Start diagramming in the browser

# draw.io documentation

> The full text of the draw.io documentation at https://www.drawio.com/docs/, one section per page, generated when the site is built. https://www.drawio.com/llms.txt is the short overview with links.

Diagrams are saved as .drawio files. Their XML is described in "The .drawio file format" (https://www.drawio.com/docs/reference/file-format/), and its XML Schema is https://www.drawio.com/mxfile.xsd.

AI assistants create draw.io diagrams through the draw.io MCP server at https://mcp.draw.io/mcp. Its create_diagram tool takes draw.io XML, Mermaid, PlantUML or CSV. create_semantic_diagram, the fast mode for flowcharts and swimlane diagrams the user asks to get quickly, takes a description of the steps, lanes and transitions that the server lays out. The MCP Tool Server (npx @drawio/mcp) also opens CSV. The tools and formats are in "Generate and validate draw.io diagrams with AI" (https://www.drawio.com/docs/reference/diagram-generation/).

# draw.io documentation

Source: https://www.drawio.com/docs/

Welcome to the draw.io documentation. 

## Quick Links

- [Getting Started](https://www.drawio.com/docs/getting-started/) - Learn the basics of technical diagramming with draw.io.
- [Using draw.io](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/) - How to use all the features of the draw.io editor, including [advanced features](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/advanced/) for power users.
- [Troubleshooting](https://www.drawio.com/docs/troubleshooting/) - Answers to specific FAQs.
- [Reference](https://www.drawio.com/docs/reference/) - Keyboard shortcuts, configuration, AI generation and plugin reference information.
- [Tutorials](https://www.drawio.com/docs/tutorials/) - In depth tutorials for various draw.io features and editor functions.
- [Types of technical diagrams](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/) - Detailed examples and how to draw them in draw.io. 
- [Diagramming best practices](https://www.drawio.com/docs/best-practice/) - Drawing and generating accessible and useful diagrams and choosing an appropriate diagramming tool.
- [Integrations](https://www.drawio.com/docs/integrations/) - Documentation for the draw.io apps for Atlassian, Google, Microsoft, Notion and other integrations.
- [Security](https://www.drawio.com/docs/security/) - Additional and technical information about how draw.io keeps your diagram data secure.

---

# About draw.io

Source: https://www.drawio.com/docs/about/

draw.io is the world's most widely used diagramming application and it's [free to use](https://app.diagrams.net) and deploy yourself.

Since 2005, we've been building diagramming software with one mission: **provide free, high quality diagramming software for everyone.**

**Your data stays yours.** We will never lock you out of your own diagrams. [Your files stay with you](https://www.drawio.com/docs/getting-started/save-diagram-files), not us.

**Free for everyone.** The draw.io editor source code is Apache 2.0 licensed. No artificial scarcity, no Enterprise tier for SSO.

**No lock-in.** When companies pay us (through our [Atlassian integrations](https://www.drawio.com/docs/integrations/atlassian/)), it's because we add value, not because we've trapped them. You always control your data.

**Independent and sustainable.** We're not VC-funded or chasing growth-at-all-costs. draw.io Ltd (UK) and draw.io AG (Switzerland) are private companies focused on building great software, not inflating valuations.

**Privacy-first.** The free [app.diagrams.net](https://app.diagrams.net) stores nothing on our servers, your diagrams stay on your device or your [chosen cloud storage](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/storage-location-select).

---

draw.io Ltd · Artisans' House, 7 Queensbridge, NN4 7BF, Northampton, UK · Registered in England #04051179

draw.io AG · Altenhofstrasse 45, 8008 Zürich, Switzerland · CHE-210.604.548

---

# An overview of draw.io's features

Source: https://www.drawio.com/docs/features/

The draw.io diagram editor on all platforms and integrations looks the same and offers the same main features no matter where you are using it. You can open a diagram created in one integration in another.

## Secure your diagram data

All of the draw.io applications and integrations with various platforms, as well as our free online diagram editor at [app.diagrams.net](https://app.diagrams.net) do not store your diagram data - draw.io is a [unique security-first diagramming tool](https://www.drawio.com/docs/security/). 

* Set [data governance options](https://www.drawio.com/docs/security/data-governance-lockdown) for fine control over extended features. 
* [Install our offline desktop app](https://get.diagrams.net/), available on Windows, MacOS and Linux.

## Store diagram files wherever you want

Use whichever cloud platform you prefer to store your diagram files: [Google Drive](https://app.diagrams.net/?mode=google), [Microsoft OneDrive](https://app.diagrams.net/?mode=onedrive), [GitHub](https://app.diagrams.net/?mode=github)/[GitLab](https://app.diagrams.net/?mode=gitlab), in your browser, or on your device.

**No account needed** - your diagrams are not locked behind an account. 

Use [our free online editor](https://app.diagrams.net) in your browser and on [mobile and touchscreen devices](https://www.drawio.com/docs/tutorials/touch-screen-diagrams).

[Image: Tap and drag a connector from the direction arrows on one shape and release over another shape to connect the two]

### Integrate diagrams with other software

Store and work with draw.io diagrams in [Atlassian Confluence](https://marketplace.atlassian.com/apps/1210933/draw-io-diagrams-for-confluence) and [Jira](https://marketplace.atlassian.com/apps/1211413/draw-io-diagrams-for-jira?hosting=cloud&tab=overview). External collaborators don't need to join your instance, they can view and edit diagram files that you share with them using our [online editor](https://app.diagrams.net) - no account or diagram format conversion is needed.

Use draw.io add-ons with [Microsoft OneDrive](https://www.drawio.com/docs/integrations/microsoft/microsoft-office-diagrams), [Google Drive](https://www.drawio.com/docs/integrations/google/google-drive-diagrams) which works with Google Workplace and [Google Classroom](https://www.drawio.com/docs/integrations/google/google-classroom-diagrams), [Google Docs, Sheets and Slides](https://www.drawio.com/docs/integrations/google/google-docs-diagrams), and [Notion](https://chrome.google.com/webstore/detail/drawio-for-notion/plhaalebpkihaccllnkdaokdoeaokmle). You can also use draw.io with many [third party integrations](https://www.drawio.com/docs/integrations)

[[Image: draw.io runs as a web app, a desktop app, a self-hosted Docker image and a Chrome app, stores diagrams in Google Drive, OneDrive, SharePoint, GitHub or on your device, and works in Google Docs, Sheets, Slides and Classroom, Microsoft Word, Excel and PowerPoint, Confluence, Jira, Microsoft Teams, SharePoint pages and Notion, and AI assistants such as Claude, ChatGPT, Codex, GitHub Copilot and Cursor.]](https://www.drawio.com/docs/integrations/)

**Advanced:** See how to [embed the draw.io editor](https://www.drawio.com/docs/tutorials/embedding-walkthrough) in your own application.

## Collaborate in real-time with shared cursors

Multiple people editing a diagram can see each others' changes **synchronised in real time** using [Google Drive](https://app.diagrams.net/?mode=google), [Microsoft OneDrive](https://app.diagrams.net/?mode=onedrive), and [draw.io in Confluence](https://marketplace.atlassian.com/apps/1210933/draw-io-diagrams-for-confluence). 

[Image: Share your mouse cursor with others who are editing the same diagram file stored in OneDrive or Google Drive]

## Easy-to-use diagram editor

The draw.io apps work just like the office and drawing tools you are familiar with.

* Drag and drop shapes from the shape libraries and drag to [draw connectors](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/connectors/connect-shapes) between them.
* Drag connectors to [change their path manually](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/connectors/waypoints-connectors) or let them reroute automatically.
* Double click and start typing to [add a label](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/text/labels-add) to anything. 
* Create [tables](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/shapes/tables/) and [swimlane flows](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/swimlane-diagrams) with a familiar tool.
* [Style shapes](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/styles/shape-styles) and [connectors](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/styles/connector-styles) with [customisable palettes](https://www.drawio.com/docs/reference/configure-diagram-editor), [fill styles](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/styles/rough-style), fonts and [text formatting](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/styles/text-styles).
* [Search for shapes](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/editor/panels/search-omnibox), including in open-source icon libraries.
* Use our vast libraries of shapes and [templates](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/templates/) to create a range of technical diagrams and infographics. 
* Enter a text description and let an [AI tool generate the diagram](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/generate).
* Diagram faster with [keyboard shortcuts](https://www.drawio.com/docs/reference/shortcuts/modifier-shortcuts-in-diagrams).  

[Image: Add a second shape and connect it from the first - hover and click on the direction arrow, or drag a shape over another and drop it on a direction arrow]

## Customise the draw.io editor

Find your favourite [editor theme](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/editor/appearance/) - a simple [online whiteboard](https://www.drawio.com/docs/getting-started/online-whiteboard), floating [tool panels](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/editor/panels/), or the standard editor layout. You can also [switch the editor to use your language](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/editor/editor-language-change).

[[Image: Sketch editor theme for a simpler online whiteboard]](https://app.diagrams.net/?splash=0&ui=sketch&title=#Uhttps%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2Fjgraph%2Fdrawio-diagrams%2Fmaster%2Fblog%2Fboard-visual-tutorial.drawio)

## Import and export many formats

Drag and drop a file to [import a diagram](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/import/), including many other [diagram formats](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/import/import-formats) and continue editing. Publish and [export to many formats](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/export/export-diagram). 

[Image: Import diagrams into an existing diagram in two different ways]

## Diagram in dark mode

The draw.io editor can automatically adjust the colours and brightness to make sure you diagram is readable when you use [dark mode](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/editor/appearance/dark-mode). You can [set user-defined colours](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/editor/appearance/adaptive-colours) to override the automatic dark-mode colours, or disable adaptive colours in the editor to have the editor panels in dark mode, but the diagram always in light mode. 

[Image: Change the adaptive colours settings on a diagram in draw.io via the Extras menu or the Style tab in the format panel when nothing is selected]

## Advanced diagramming tools

Many advanced and helpful tools are built into the diagram editor.

* Use the infinite canvas, rulers, [customisable grid](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/editor/panels/editor-grid-change) and positioning guidelines to help you diagram faster.
* Let [auto-layouts](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/editor/menus/arrange-layout-menu) format flowcharts and tree diagrams for you.
* Organise your diagram with [layers](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/layers/) and [tags](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/links-tooltips-tags/tags-in-diagrams). Set [shape properties](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/shapes/shape-properties), [metadata](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/shapes/shape-metadata) and [placeholders](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/advanced/placeholders) to add [translations](https://www.drawio.com/docs/tutorials/translate-diagrams), [tooltips](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/links-tooltips-tags/tooltips), [links](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/links-tooltips-tags/custom-links), and interactive actions.
* Sketch and comment with [freehand shapes](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/shapes/freehand-drawing).

[Image: Use the freehand drawing tool in a draw.io Board diagram to markup diagrams or draw shapes with your mouse]

* Create your own [custom shapes](https://www.drawio.com/docs/tutorials/custom-shapes) and [custom shape libraries](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/advanced/custom-shape-libraries).
* [Format text with HTML](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/styles/text-styles) and use [mathematics typesetting](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/text/math-typesetting) in labels.
* Generate diagrams text using [Mermaid code](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/mermaid/), [CSV spreadsheet data](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/import/insert-from-csv) and formatting information, or [SQL code](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/insert/insert-sql).
* [Customise the editor](https://www.drawio.com/docs/reference/configure-diagram-editor) to set a specific palette, custom fonts, templates, shape libraries, and more. 

**Tip:** If you use draw.io in Confluence, administrators can [mass import all the Gliffy diagrams](https://www.drawio.com/docs/integrations/atlassian/confluence/mass-import-gliffy-confluence-cloud) in your instance in one step.

## Create a wide range of technical diagrams

Our shape libraries let you create whatever type of diagram you need: 
* [floorplans](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/floorplans), [org charts](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/org-charts), [process flows](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/bpmn-2-0) and [network infrastructures](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/network-diagrams)
* [infographics](https://www.drawio.com/docs/tutorials/infographics-layered-shapes), [story maps](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/story-mapping) and [timelines](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/timeline-diagrams)
* [UML diagrams](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/uml/), [kanban boards](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/kanban-boards), [entity relationship models](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/entity-relationship-tables) and [fishbone diagrams](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/ishikawa-diagrams)
* [circuit diagrams](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/shapes/waypoint-shape), [rack diagrams](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/rack-diagrams), [attack trees](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/threat-modelling) and [dependency graphs](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/dependency-graphs)
* ... and [many more](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/)

[[Image: Activity diagrams are used to model workflows in various ways]](https://viewer.diagrams.net/?lightbox=1&highlight=0000ff&edit=_blank&page=1&layers=1&nav=1&title=#Uhttps%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2Fjgraph%2Fdrawio-diagrams%2Fdev%2Fexamples%2Fuml-activity-example.drawio) [[Image: A floorplan created in draw.io]](https://viewer.diagrams.net/?lightbox=1&highlight=0000ff&edit=_blank&layers=1&nav=1&title=#Uhttps%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2Fjgraph%2Fdrawio-diagrams%2Fdev%2Fexamples%2FFloorplan.xml) 

[[Image: Enterprise business model template]](https://viewer.diagrams.net/?lightbox=1&highlight=0000ff&edit=_blank&layers=1&nav=1&title=#Uhttps%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2Fjgraph%2Fdrawio-diagrams%2Fdev%2Ftemplates%2Fbusiness%2Flean_mapping_2.xml) [[Image: An example BPMN diagram]](https://viewer.diagrams.net/?splash=0&ui=kennedy&ibs=bpmn2&title=#Uhttps%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2Fjgraph%2Fdrawio-diagrams%2Fdev%2Fexamples%2FBPMN.xml)

[[Image: Use waypoint shapes in draw.io to show contact points in electrical circuit diagrams]](https://viewer.diagrams.net/?lightbox=1&highlight=0000ff&edit=_blank&layers=1&nav=1&title=#Uhttps%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2Fjgraph%2Fdrawio-diagrams%2Fdev%2Fexamples%2Fcircuit-logic-examples.drawio) [[Image: A simple rack diagram, created with draw.io]](https://viewer.diagrams.net/?lightbox=1&highlight=0000ff&edit=_blank&layers=1&nav=1&title=#Uhttps%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2Fjgraph%2Fdrawio-diagrams%2Fdev%2Fexamples%2Frack-diagram-simple-server.drawio)

# Diagramming best practices

Source: https://www.drawio.com/docs/best-practice/

Technical diagrams are used in almost all professional fields as planning and compliance records, user manuals, project documentation, business process descriptions, manufacturing procedures, design plans for both digital and physical products and spaces, and much more. 

It can be tricky to decide on a diagramming tool, know which type of diagram to use when, and to draw easy-to-understand diagrams. Here are a collection of articles that may help.

# Consistency in diagrams

Source: https://www.drawio.com/docs/best-practice/consistent-diagrams/

Diagrams can convey a lot of information at a glance, but only if they follow the three C's - for drawing technical diagrams that means `concise`, `clear` and `consistent`. As the diagram author, you are responsible for _clarity_ and _conciseness_. For _consistency_ however, draw.io has many tools to help you draw diagrams that are easier to read.

Consistency makes technical diagrams easier to read.

Inconsistent diagrams can cause confusion and annoy your audience. But in the worst case, they could cause serious misunderstandings, processes followed incorrectly, or wrong implementations and a finished product that does not meet its requirements.

## Draw consistent diagrams

The [principles of grouping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principles_of_grouping) explain how humans see objects organised into patterns. While there are some slight [cultural differences in perception](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_precedence), consistent alignment, styles and shapes allow people to comprehend what they see more quickly and clearly.

### Consistent shapes

Use the same shape for the same type of element in your diagram. This is especially important when there are official or de facto standards for the type of diagram you are drawing. 

For example: 
* Use a rounded rectangle for all steps in a flow chart and a diamond for choices. 
* Click on _More Shapes_ in the shapes panel and enable the shape libraries for standard shapes - [BPMN](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/bpmn-2-0), [C4](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/c4-modelling), [AWS](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/aws-diagrams), etc.

In the example below, you can see a [Citrix](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/citrix-diagrams) Hybrid Multi-Cloud manages AWS and GCP clouds within the same infrastructure, where shapes from each of the platform's shape libraries have been used.

[Image: Use appropriate shapes for each infrastructure provider with the draw.io shape libraries]

**Create your own library**

If you have an internal diagram standard or corporate style, you can create your own [custom shape library](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/advanced/custom-shape-libraries) and share it with your team. 

### Consistent shape sizes

Consistent sizes help us pattern match when reading a diagram. Make all the elements of your diagram of the same type also the same size in a couple of steps.

1. Select the source shape that is the size you want to use, then click _Copy Size_ in the _Arrange_ tab of the format panel.
2. Select the shape you want to resize, and click _Paste Size_.

[Image: Copy and paste a selected shape's size to quickly resize other shapes]

The height and width of the selected shapes will now match the one you copied, even if they are different shapes.

### Consistent shape colours and styles

Just as you used the same shapes for the same type of object or step, you should use the same [shape styles](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/styles/shape-styles). When using colour coding or shape outline styles to add meaning to your diagram, make sure the same meaning applies throughout your diagram. 

Select a shape or connector and then click _Set default style_ in the _Style_ tab of the format panel. Every subsequent shape or connector you add to the drawing canvas will use that default style. 

You can also [copy and paste styles](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/styles/styles-copy-paste).

### Consistent connector styles and arrow heads

Use different [connector styles](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/styles/connector-styles) to indicate different groupings. For example, a dotted or dashed connector could indicate an optional step in a flow chart, or an externally provided service in an infrastructure diagram.

**Restyle multiple selected connectors**

1. Right click on the drawing canvas to show the context menu and _Select Edges_ to select all connectors. Alternatively, hold ``Shift`` and click on each connector you want to include. 
2. Select the arrow heads, line styles and thickness you want to use for all selected connectors. 

[Image: Style your connector using the options in the Style tab in the format panel on the right in draw.io]

### Consistent positioning

In general, humans innately prefer designs that are symmetrical and organised. The brain is wired to quickly recognise patterns - a consistently aligned diagram is easier for the brain to process.

For example, neatly aligned and equally spaced process steps ensures there is no confusion over the order in which they must be implemented. Space between grouped devices can visually indicate they are on different subnetworks. 

Enable the [drawing grid, snap-to-grid option and the guidelines](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/editor/panels/diagram-options) to help you align shapes and connectors as you move them around the drawing canvas. 

Select multiple shapes and use the alignment tools in the _Arrange_ tab of the format panel to [space and align shapes in just a couple of clicks](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/shapes/arrange-align-shapes)
[Image: draw.io has alignment and distribute tools that let you neaten diagrams quickly and easily]

### Consistent labelling

Use consistent fonts, font sizes, text styles (italic, bold), spacing, and label positions via the _Text_ tab of the format panel. Keep the text as concise and accurate as possible. 

[Image: Select a shape, then select the Text tab in the format panel to change its style]

Consistent naming conventions will also help your audience read your diagram. For all labels: 
* all plurals
* all singular words
* following a pattern like 'verb + noun'
* with consistent numbering

[Image: An example communication diagram of the sequence diagram]

See how to [style text](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/styles/text-styles) and [add labels to any diagram](https://www.drawio.com/docs/tutorials/label-any-diagram)

## Tips for easy-to-read diagrams

If you have drawn a complex diagram or used many abbreviations, include a legend to reduce the risk of misunderstanding. 

Ensure your diagram elements are all at the same level of abstraction. Typically, a diagram should be low-level and detailed, or a high-level overview, and not both.

# Diagramming tools

Source: https://www.drawio.com/docs/best-practice/diagramming-tools/

Humans understand information faster and more easily in diagrams. This is why there are many visualisation tools, from simple sketching apps, to single-purpose diagramming tools and whiteboarding apps, through to technical drawing applications like draw.io and hyper-specialised CAD and architectural tools for precision drawings. 

## Choose a tool for your needs

So, which type of diagramming tool should you use?

### Basic sketching and drawing

The most basic of drawing tools are illustration programs like MS Paint where you can draw simple free-form sketches. 

It is not easy to use these illustration applications - even feature-rich apps like Procreate - to create the more precise technical diagrams needed for business, IT, or industry documentation, especially when you need to use a standardised notation. 

Illustration tools are usually single-user, saving files to your device or a mounted cloud storage location, with no support for collaboration.

However, as their toolset is so easy to use, you can quickly sketch a version of a user interface, infographic layout, or presentation graphic and evaluate a colour scheme or text block placement.

[[Image: Freehand drawing in draw.io on a tablet - click the freehand tool in the toolbar on the left]](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/shapes/freehand-drawing)

_While you can draw [freehand shapes](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/shapes/freehand-drawing) in draw.io, you won't have the brush, style and palette freedom of an illustration app._

### Whiteboarding

The next level of sophistication includes whiteboarding tools like Miro as well as specialised applications for specific types of diagrams, for example mind-mapping with Mind Meister, simple infographics and cover spreads with Canva, or mobile app mockups with Figma. 

These tools are designed for [online collaboration](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/collaboration/concurrent-editing), usually charging a per-user subscription fee for commercial use. Diagram files are stored either in the whiteboarding app's cloud or on one of the popular cloud storage platforms. 

To ensure an online whiteboard is conveniently available for project meetings, the apps are often integrated with other remote team software products, such as how Miro integrates with Zoom and Slack. A range of generic meeting and presentation templates can speed up meeting preparation.

You can use whiteboarding apps in the same way as a physical whiteboard: for brainstorming, mocking up layouts or workflows, or [planning and tracking projects](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/use-cases/project-planning-diagrams) just as you would with sticky notes in person. 

[Image: Brainstorm and plan projects on an online whiteboard with sketch.diagrams.net]

_The [Sketch whiteboard editor theme](https://www.drawio.com/docs/getting-started/online-whiteboard) simplified the visible interface to make the drawing canvas less intimidating, but it still works as a technical diagramming tool - all the draw.io features are there inside the toolbar on the left._

## Technical diagramming

This is the broadest category of diagramming apps, where drawing tools start to get a bit more complex. 

Apps like draw.io have the advanced features, extensive shape libraries and tools you need to draw formal diagrams for professional documentation, including network and cloud architectures, [BPMN diagrams](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/bpmn-2-0) and flowcharts, UML diagrams, business hierarchies, relational models, state diagrams, data and control flows, and many more specific [use cases for different professions](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/use-cases). 

These diagrams require more precision and structure than a standard whiteboarding app can provide, as well as a library of standardised notations and shapes to cover the variety of technical diagrams used in documentation. 

[[Image: An example BPMN diagram that details the steps involved in processing an order]](https://app.diagrams.net/?splash=0&ui=kennedy&ibs=bpmn2&title=#Uhttps%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2Fjgraph%2Fdrawio-diagrams%2Fmaster%2Fblog%2Fbpmn-2-example.drawio)

Technical diagramming tools often support real-time collaboration, and have been integrated into many documentation platforms. 

Note that some of these tools may lock your diagram data behind accounts and/or subscriptions, which can impede the collaboration aspect.  With draw.io, you [choose where to store your diagram files](https://www.drawio.com/docs/getting-started/save-diagram-files) and all your team members and external partners can use the editor freely.

## Precise CAD and architecture modelling

At the most complex end of the diagramming tools spectrum are the industry-specific CAD modelling tools and architecture software. Precision and accuracy, scale, and extreme detail are important in tools like AutoCAD, and usually require extensive user training.

This type of diagramming software is primarily used by mechanical and civil engineers, interior designers and architects, and in the construction industry, where 2D diagrams for documentation are generated automatically from a complete and detailed 3D model.

[[Image: A ground floor apartment floorplan created in draw.io]](https://app.diagrams.net/?lightbox=1&highlight=0000ff&edit=_blank&layers=1&nav=1&title=#Uhttps%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2Fjgraph%2Fdrawio-diagrams%2Fdev%2Fblog%2Ffloorplan-apartment.drawio) 

_You can use draw.io for floorplans, but they aren't to scale, and therefore not fit for use as a construction blueprint. They work well for planning an office, conference or apartment furniture layout, or to draw an evacuation or LAN map._

[See how to draw a floorplan in draw.io](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/floorplans)

## When an app supports multiple levels of diagramming complexity

While many tools have features that let you create diagrams of various types and complexities, they were all designed _primarily_ for users at one of the levels described above. 

While you _can_ [sketch elaborate freehand shapes](https://www.drawio.com/docs/tutorials/draw-infographics) in draw.io, use it as a [whiteboard](https://www.drawio.com/docs/getting-started/online-whiteboard), or draw a 2D engineering models line-by-line, it would be more complicated and slower than if you used a diagramming tool designed for those specific types of diagrams. But if you are used to the draw.io editor, you may find this faster than learning a new, more specific application.

draw.io is [designed for technical diagrams](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/), using the collection of shape libraries and custom libraries to draw whatever visual documentation of systems, processes, hierarchies, data and states you need.

### Further considerations

When choosing a diagramming tool, also consider the following:
- whether you need [real-time collaboration](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/collaboration/concurrent-editing) features
- if [integrations](https://www.drawio.com/docs/integrations) to make diagramming more convenient exist for your documentation platform
- where your diagram data is to be stored
- if version control is required
- whether access is gated behind accounts or subscriptions
- whether there are configuration options to [lockdown access to diagram data](https://www.drawio.com/docs/security/data-governance-lockdown)
- if [editor customisations](https://www.drawio.com/docs/reference/configure-diagram-editor) will help you diagram faster
- whether [AI generation](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/generate/) is feasible and needs to be [built into your development workflow](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/generate/drawio-mcp-server)
- whether you or your team mates prefer to work in [dark mode](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/editor/appearance/dark-mode)
- whether the application has [keyboard or modifier shortcuts](https://www.drawio.com/docs/reference/shortcuts/) that will make diagramming faster and easier

# Diagram, chart or graph?

Source: https://www.drawio.com/docs/best-practice/diagrams-charts-graphs/

Have you been asked to create a chart, a diagram, or a graph? There is a lot of confusion around these overlapping terms, especially as they are most often used interchangeably. However, there are some minor differences in how they are used.

Here's a rough guide to the difference between charts, graphs, diagrams, figures, plots, maps, and models. 

## Diagrams

You could think of diagrams as the super-category: Anything that [visualises information in an abstract way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diagram) is a diagram. For example, an image with labels, a tree diagram categorising items, a floor plan, an infographic, an electrical wiring diagram, a process flow, and so on.

A good rule of thumb for using more specific terms - when the visualisation is driven by a numerical data set, chart, graph or plot will be more accurate.

## Graphs

**Graphs** usually represent quantitative data on an 2D image with an x-y axis, using lines or bars. Graphs can visualise numerical data or a mathematical function, and are often generated from data in a spreadsheet.

The word 'graph' is used outside of this context. For example, infographics explain complex topics in simple abstract visualisations, and [dependency graphs](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/dependency-graphs) show relationships between various elements.
[[Image: Dependency graph of the draw.io website on GitHub]](https://app.diagrams.net/?lightbox=1&highlight=0000ff&edit=_blank&layers=1&nav=1&title=#Uhttps%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2Fjgraph%2Fdrawio-diagrams%2Fdev%2Fexamples%2Fgemfile-dependency-graph.drawio)

### Plots

**Plots** are not as often encountered. They are generated from a numerical data set and commonly used in mathematics, finance, and engineering. Individual data points are plotted on a 2D or 3D axis, for example, as a scatterplot.

## Charts

**Charts** also represent quantitative data. Charts can be graphs (line charts), but some aren't (pie charts). Many charts put quantitative data on one axis, and categories (qualitative data) on the other axis.

However, the word 'chart' is also used to refer to several other types of diagrams (that often don't display quantitative data): flowcharts, Gantt charts, organisation charts, and relationship charts.

[Image: An example BPMN diagram that details the steps involved in processing an order]

## Figures

**Figure** has so many different meanings that depend on the context in which it is used. The most common usage refers to any image, drawing, graph, diagram, chart or plot in a reference book, scientific paper, or digital resource.

The word 'figure' can also be used to mean 'number' - e.g. a figure 8, or a table of sales figures.

## Maps and models and plans

To complicate matters even more, **maps**, **models** and **plans** are also words used to refer to specific types of diagrams. 

* [Story mapping](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/story-mapping) and [roadmaps](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/timeline-diagrams) are used in product marketing, and mindmaps are used to explore subject areas when brainstorming.
* [C4 models](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/c4-modelling) describe and define IT architectures, [application threat models](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/threat-modelling) are used to explore infrastructure risks, and wireframe models can represent physical objects or the layout of a digital product.
* [Floorplans or floormaps](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/floorplans) show the layout of an indoor space. 

<a href="https://app.diagrams.net/?lightbox=1&highlight=0000ff&edit=_blank&layers=1&nav=1&title=threat-modelling.drawio#Uhttps%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2Fjgraph%2Fdrawio-diagrams%2Fmaster%2Fblog%2Fthreat-modelling.drawio">[Image: Example data flow diagram for threat modelling]</a>

## Templates for all types of diagrams

Our draw.io apps come with many templates, [organised into categories in the template library](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/templates/template-diagrams) roughly corresponding to the terms described above. 

[Image: Hover over a template in draw.io to see a larger preview of it]

1. Select _Arrange > Insert > Template_ to open the template library. 
2. Browse the categories on the left and select a template on the right. Click on the magnifying glass to see a larger preview. 
3. Click _Insert_ to add it to the drawing canvas. 

**Tip:** You can also [generate a diagram](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/generate/) from a text description of your particular diagram. 
- click on _Generate_ in the _Basic_ section of the library
- click on the _Generate_ button in the toolbar to open the _Generate_ dialog.
- describe your diagram in text in the search field and select _Generate_.

## Shapes for different types of diagrams

You can create abstract line charts and bar graphs using the _Infographic_ shape library. However, as the draw.io editor is not connected to a form of numerical data input, creating exact graphs from quantitative data is better done in a spreadsheet. 

[Image: Enable the Infographic shape library to create abstract graphs and charts]

1. Click on _More Shapes_ at the bottom of the Shapes panel. 
2. Enable the checkboxes next to the shape libraries you want to use, and click _Apply_.

# When does it make sense to generate a diagram?

Source: https://www.drawio.com/docs/best-practice/generated-diagrams/

In draw.io, you can [generate a diagram](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/generate) from a text description. It's quick, easy and requires almost no fiddly positioning of shapes and connectors.

It's easy to get hyped up about quickly generating visual documentation, but when _should_ you generate a technical diagram? What types of diagrams can't be generated? 

[Image: When should you use a diagram generator to draw technical diagrams?]

[_Open this diagram in draw.io_](https://app.diagrams.net/?lightbox=1&highlight=0000ff&edit=_blank&page=0&layers=1&nav=1&title=#Uhttps%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2Fjgraph%2Fdrawio-diagrams%2Fdev%2Fblog%2Fdiagram-generation.drawio)

First, let's see how smart templates work in draw.io.

**Generate a diagram**

1. Select _Arrange > Insert > Generate_ or click on the _Generate_ tool (sparkle button in the toolbar), or select _+ > Generate_.
  * Alternatively, start a new diagram and click on _Generate_ in the template library.
  * Start typing a description in the [search field](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/editor/panels/search-omnibox). 
2. Write a simple and accurate text description of your diagram, then click _Generate_
3. Hover over the diagram preview to preview it. 
   * If you like what you see, click _Add_. 

[Image: Generate a diagram with Smart Templates in draw.io]

Now, you can edit, add to and style your generated diagram freely using the draw.io shape libraries and format panel. 

Learn more about [generating diagrams in draw.io](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/generate) and [how to write a good query](https://www.drawio.com/docs/best-practice/write-query-generate-diagram). 

## When to draw a diagram manually

It's probably easier to explain when _not_ to generate a diagram using an AI tool.

### Using notation standards

Diagram generators output mostly simple shapes - rectangles, lifelines, circles, connectors and so on. If you need [BPMN](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/bpmn-2-0) process flows, [C4 models](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/c4-modelling), [AWS](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/aws-diagrams) or GCP network diagrams, and so on, enable the appropriate shape libraries in draw.io, and draw your diagram manually so it follows that technical standard. 

**Note:** UML sequence and state diagrams may be an exception here - there are enough examples in most generator's training set that they can produce reasonable _generic_ diagrams.

[Image: Generate a UML sequence diagram from a text description via the template library in draw.io] [Image: Generate a state diagram from a text description via the template library in draw.io]

### Existing systems or processes

Diagram generation in draw.io can only work from your short text description - it does not know any information about your existing infrastructure or processes. Therefore, it can't draw accurate technical diagrams to document existing code, systems, workflows or networks, or interfaces to other systems and external processes. 

### Unsupported diagram types

There are many types of technical and business oriented diagrams that are not supported by generators - fishbone cause/effect diagrams, rack diagrams, interface mockups, Kanban boards, infographics and other marketing diagrams (5C, SWOT, PEST), timelines and roadmaps, and many more [technical diagram use cases](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/use-cases) that you can use draw.io for.

**Tip:** Most of the diagram types supported by Mermaid syntax are supported by diagram generators. If you have a preferred diagram generator outside of draw.io, ask it to export Mermaid code - you can then [insert the Mermaid code into draw.io](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/mermaid/) and then edit and style your generated diagram afterwards. 

## When to generate a diagram

Generated diagrams can be useful to brainstorm _generic components_ of a system, or outline a _common workflow_, or draw a _mindmap of a concept_, perhaps to plan for an event or structure a document or presentation. 

For example, you could ask it to generate a flowchart of a "``browser-based file storage system using a serverless AWS pattern``". 

[Image: Generate a state diagram from a text description via the template library in draw.io]

It won't be correct, or have precise details of the system, or even use the correct shapes. But it may give you a general starting point that you can then use to draw your actual system. 

## Limitations of generated diagrams

### Illogical AI hallucinations

Keep in mind that diagram generators do not sanity check anything in your diagram - there may be completely illogical elements. 

When asked to generate a flowchart or decision tree for the query "``When does it make sense to use AI to generate a diagram``", the generated decision flow is fairly high level. But it does correctly report that complex diagrams, or diagrams of existing systems can't be generated by AI.
  
[Image: There are some logical problems with this generated flowchart]

### No knowledge of existing systems
The biggest limitation for technical diagrams for documentation purposes is that diagram generators do not know about your existing system and processes, and therefore any diagram you try to generate will not be accurate.

### Can't use corporate style

Generators also won't use your corporate style, specific layouts preferred by your team, or a diagramming standard that needs specific shapes, labels and connectors. 

### Can't edit existing diagram data

Most generators, including the draw.io smart templates feature, don't have any memory of previous attempts, so they can't refine an already generated diagram. Regenerating starts over from scratch every time.

Generating multiple iterations and hoping for a usable diagram that you can then clean up may be slower than manually drawing your diagram from scratch. 

## Related

Learn more about [generating diagrams in draw.io](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/generate), how to [enable generated diagrams in the Atlassian draw.io apps](https://www.drawio.com/docs/integrations/atlassian/confluence/customise/confluence-cloud-enable-diagram-generation), and see [examples of generated diagrams](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/generate/generated-diagrams-examples).

New to diagramming or to draw.io? The [getting started guide](https://www.drawio.com/docs/getting-started/) and [simple flowchart tutorial](https://www.drawio.com/docs/getting-started/basic-flowchart) will get you up and running. 

For more technical diagram examples and use cases, check the [diagram gallery](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/), or the [template library](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/templates/) in draw.io. There are many more templates and examples in the [drawio-diagrams repository on GitHub](https://github.com/jgraph/drawio-diagrams).

# A history of diagram search terms

Source: https://www.drawio.com/docs/best-practice/popular-diagram-searches/

Diagrams are growing in popularity worldwide, and search trends reflect this in interesting ways. By comparing various search phrases in Google Trends, we can see that "how to diagram" has been pretty stable over the past 20 years. But now, people are also searching for which type of diagram to use and when they would be best put to use. 

[Image: Search trends clearly show that more people know that diagrams are useful and now need to know what type of diagram to use]

Let's dig a little deeper into these diagramming search trends. 

## Flowcharts, mind maps or org charts?
Of the three most popular types of diagrams used in organisations, especially in meetings, which would win out of flowcharts, mind maps or organisation charts? 

Unsurprisingly, [flowcharts](https://www.drawio.com/docs/getting-started/basic-flowchart) are the most popular - they are used to document processes in all types of industries and teams. 

[Image: Flowcharts are more popular than mind maps and org charts]

[BPMN diagrams](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/bpmn-2-0), cross-functional flowcharts and [swimlane diagrams](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/swimlane-diagrams), dataflow diagrams, [gitflows](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/gitflow-diagram), and value stream maps are more specialised forms of flowcharts, and all searched for at roughly the same rate.

[Image: An example BPMN diagram that details the steps involved in processing an order]

_BPMN diagrams are more structured than flowcharts_

## Which teams diagram the most?
If you work in this field, you'll not be surprised that IT diagrams are the leading search phrase, much more than business diagrams, marketing diagrams and training diagrams all combined. 

[Image: Diagrams in IT are more often searched for than business, marketing and training diagrams combined]

It's mostly likely because software and technology is increasingly more complex, and therefore easier to document visually in diagrams. But many other [professionals need to draw diagrams](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/use-cases/). 

## Different types of diagrams in IT

It was a little surprising to see [network diagrams](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/network-diagrams) decrease in the long term search trend, but perhaps people are now searching more often for cloud infrastructure diagrams. Or perhaps network management tools are automatically documenting their infrastructure for them.

[Image: While UML and network diagrams are less often searched for, mockups and user flows are becoming more popular]

[UML diagrams](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/uml/) have been losing popularity over time - they can be quite time consuming to draw and maintain for complex software products. When looking at the different types of UML diagrams, class diagrams are still regularly searched for.

[Image: A class diagram based on the basic class diagram template in draw.io]

Reflecting today's faster software development and release cycles, the search trends clearly show that mockups and user flows are increasingly popular.

[[Image: The best way to control which feature flags are enabled or disabled, and set user target segment rules is via a visual interface]](https://app.diagrams.net/?lightbox=1&highlight=0000ff&edit=_blank&layers=1&nav=1&page=1&title=#Uhttps%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2Fjgraph%2Fdrawio-diagrams%2Fdev%2Fblog%2Ffeature-flag-control-interface-mockup.drawio)

_Mockups - like this feature-flag control panel - are easily created in draw.io_

## Business diagrams for project management

The most popular business diagrams searched for are used to explore and justify business and project management decisions. 

[[Image: The structure of an Ishikawa diagram resembles a fish skeleton, where the ribs are the categories and their sub-branches are root-causes, all leading to the problem or defect on the right]](https://viewer.diagrams.net/?lightbox=1&highlight=0000ff&edit=_blank&layers=1&nav=1&page=3&title=#Uhttps%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2Fjgraph%2Fdrawio-diagrams%2Fmaster%2Fblog%2Fishikawa-diagram-examples.drawio)

# Process map, model or flowchart?

Source: https://www.drawio.com/docs/best-practice/process-map-flowchart/

There are many terms for diagrams that show a series of steps and decisions - flowchart, process diagram, process map, workflow, and process model. While many sources claim large differences between these terms, in practice, they are used interchangeably.

[Image: Flowchart and process model shapes are in the General and Flowchart shape libraries in draw.io]

## Flow diagrams

Flow diagrams can be used to show how various types of 'things' move through a process or system: data, control, materials, systems, users, tasks, and so on. 

They are used to document all the steps and decisions, and inputs and outputs of a process, aiming to achieve one or more of the following:
* train new employees faster
* optimise or standardise a repeating process
* debug errors or quality problems
* define task and decision roles and responsibilities
* document processes for security and quality accreditation purposes

## Difference between flowcharts and process models

The consensus seems to use ``flowcharts``  and ``workflows`` to refer to the more basic diagrams, and ``process models`` or ``process maps`` for the more complex diagrams, especially those that use standardised notations. 

``Process mapping`` is the act of drawing these diagrams and documenting business and system processes in great detail.

### Basic flowchart shapes

Flowcharts got their own [ANSI standard](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/367651.367657) in the 1960s, which was then incorporated into the [ISO 5807 standard](https://www.iso.org/standard/11955.html) in the 1980s, last reviewed in 2019.

The basic flowchart shapes are available in the _General_ shape library, which is enabled by default in draw.io. 

For shapes that represent magnetic tapes, punch cards, punch tapes, and other types of data storage, enable the _Flowchart_ shape library. 
* Click _More Shapes_ at the bottom of the shapes panel to select the shape libraries you want to use. 

[Image: Flowchart and process model shapes are in the General and Flowchart shape libraries in draw.io]

**Ovals** - indicate the start and end of a process. Often an open oval for the start, and a closed or double oval for the end, but sometimes drawn as a circle or a rectangle with rounded ends. 

**Rectangles** - show tasks or steps in a process, usually drawn with sharp corners to distinguish them from start/stop. A step can be another entire process, and with draw.io linked to a second diagram page to fully document that flow. 

**Diamonds** - indicate decisions, usually showing only two paths and a yes/no or true/false question. 

Connectors with arrows at one end join these shapes together to show the paths through the process.

[Image: A selection of shapes available in draw.io commonly used in flow charts]

**Tip:** Use whichever colours make your diagram easier to understand.

### Extended flowchart shapes

* Rhomboid - data input or displayed output
* Rectangle with vertical bars - a subprocess defined in another diagram
* Cylinder - a data store, database or disk drive
* Rectangle with a wavy base - one or more documents
* Trapezoid - a manual process performed by hand
* Rectangle with a sloping top - manual input step
* Hexagon - preparation or initialisation steps
* Pentagon - the target step is on another page/in another diagram
* Solid or double bar - a fork or split in a process into parallel steps. Also used to join separate paths in a process together.

[Image: A selection of shapes available in draw.io commonly used in flow charts]

[Follow this tutorial to create a basic flowchart in draw.io](https://www.drawio.com/docs/getting-started/basic-flowchart)

For complex flowchart template examples, see the _Flowcharts_ section in the template manager (_Arrange > Insert > Template_ via the menu or _+ > Template_ in the toolbar)

[Image: Flowchart and process model shapes are in the General and Flowchart shape libraries in draw.io]

## Vertical or horizontal?

Use whichever layout for your flowchart or process model that is easiest for your audience to read and understand. 

For example, use a vertical flow for printed documentation, and horizontal for when it needs to be enlarged and taped to a wall above an assembly line.

**Multilingual diagrams:** Keep in mind that some languages are read top down or right to left. To avoid confusion, use clear **start** and **end** shapes when drawing a diagram that will be translated.

The [automatic layout shapes](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/shapes/automated-layout-shapes) in the _Advanced_ shape library can help you assemble a flowchart quickly.

[Image: Hold down alt as you click on shapes in the shape library to add and connect them inside a automatic flow layout shape]

Alternatively, [generate a diagram](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/generate) in draw.io from a description of your process. Here's how to [write a good query to generate a diagram](https://www.drawio.com/docs/best-practice/write-query-generate-diagram).

## Detailed and complex process diagrams

[Swimlane diagrams](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/swimlane-diagrams), cross-functional flowcharts or deployment flowcharts all use lanes to indicate the actors or systems that perform the steps and decisions in a flow. Use a [cross-functional table](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/shapes/tables/) in draw.io to draw a process with swimlanes easily. 

[Image: The basic cross-functional flowchart template after being styled, as provided in the draw.io template manager]

[BPMN diagrams](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/bpmn-2-0) are one of the more complex types of flowcharts and follow the [BPMN 2 notation standard](http://www.omg.org/spec/BPMN/2.0/). Choreography models show the interaction between people throughout a process, and orchestration diagrams show the task order. Most BPMN diagrams are a combination of these two flows.
* Specific icons are attached to traditional flowchart rectangles to indicate types of tasks. 
* Circular shapes are used in between tasks to show a wide range of events, both 'catching' and 'throwing'. 
* Diamond gateway shapes indicate decisions, where paths split and merge. 
* Pools containing swimlanes are used to group the teams and roles responsible for each step, event and decision in a process.

[[Image: An example BPMN diagram that details the steps involved in processing an order]](https://viewer.diagrams.net/?splash=0&ibs=bpmn2&title=#Uhttps%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2Fjgraph%2Fdrawio-diagrams%2Fmaster%2Fblog%2Fbpmn-2-example.drawio)

## Related diagram types

Don't confuse flowcharts with [process flow diagrams](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/engineering-process-flow-diagrams) that are used in chemical engineering. Also called PFD diagrams or process flow sheets, these typically show piping, equipment, operation data, and process and recycling streams. 

[[Image: The process engineering shape library is used to show the production process of a sourdough bread loaf]](https://viewer.diagrams.net/?lightbox=1&highlight=0000ff&edit=_blank&layers=1&nav=1&page=4&title=#Uhttps%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2Fjgraph%2Fdrawio-diagrams%2Fdev%2Fblog%2Fsourdough-process.drawio)

However, some IT security sources now use this term (PFD) for one of the diagrams used in [threat modelling](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/threat-modelling). 

[[Image: Example process flow diagram for threat modelling]](https://app.diagrams.net/?lightbox=1&highlight=0000ff&edit=_blank&layers=1&page=1&nav=1&title=threat-modelling.drawio#Uhttps%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2Fjgraph%2Fdrawio-diagrams%2Fmaster%2Fblog%2Fthreat-modelling.drawio)

[Data flow diagrams](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/data-flow-diagrams) use a more limited set of shapes to show how data is passed between processes, datastores and external actors or systems.

[[Image: Data flow diagrams are simple to draw and show how data moves around in a system]](https://viewer.diagrams.net/?lightbox=1&highlight=0000ff&edit=_blank&layers=1&nav=1&title=#Uhttps%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2Fjgraph%2Fdrawio-diagrams%2Fdev%2Fblog%2Fdata-flow.drawio)

[UML activity diagrams](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/uml/activity-diagrams) and [sequence diagrams](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/uml/sequence-diagrams) model flows of information and control through a system or program. 

[[Image: Activity diagrams are used to model workflows in various ways]](https://viewer.diagrams.net/?lightbox=1&highlight=0000ff&edit=_blank&page=0&layers=1&nav=1&title=#Uhttps%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2Fjgraph%2Fdrawio-diagrams%2Fdev%2Fexamples%2Fuml-activity-example.drawio)

# Diagrams in technical documents

Source: https://www.drawio.com/docs/best-practice/technical-documents-diagrams/

Technical diagrams are a form of documentation by themselves. But they are also used to supplement text in many other types of documents created by technical writers and documentation teams. While some teams may have graphics designers responsible for the diagramming, tech writers may be less familiar.

[Many professions need to draw specific technical diagrams](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/use-cases), but docs teams are often required to write and diagram across many different fields. 

As a useful overview for such docs teams, what types of technical documents commonly include technical diagrams?

_All technical diagrams on this page were created in draw.io._

## User documentation

User documentation includes usage instructions for a software application or app, or for a physical product. The most common diagrams found in these documents are flowcharts, labelled mock-ups or photos and explanatory infographics.

1. **Installation guides and software user manuals** - flowcharts, [labelled interface mock-ups](https://www.drawio.com/docs/tutorials/label-any-diagram)
2. **Product manuals** - labelled diagrams and photos, flowcharts, infographics
3. **User safety information**  - flowcharts, safety hazard infographics
4. **Troubleshooting** - [tables](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/shapes/tables/), flowcharts

If your user documentation is available digitally, [add links](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/insert/insert-text-link) to shapes in your diagram so users can navigate directly to the information they require. This is particularly useful for troubleshooting instructions.

## Technical diagramming best practices

The best practices for technical documentation also apply to technical diagrams:

* Keep documentation and diagrams together in a central place - have one source of truth. 
* Track diagram changes with versioning.
* Have a regular review process to ensure diagrams are kept up to date or archived. 
* Keep diagrams as simple and as clear as possible so they are easy to read.
* Follow a style guide or use a notation standard to help with [consistency](https://www.drawio.com/docs/best-practice/consistent-diagrams) for certain types of diagrams.
* If you [generate diagrams](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/generate), make sure you check them thoroughly for accuracy.

# What makes a good UML diagram tool?

Source: https://www.drawio.com/docs/best-practice/uml-diagram-tools/

There are a wide range of UML diagramming tools available, as standalone applications, as online-only cloud software, and embedded in various content platforms. Some take text input to generate diagrams, and others are specialised to draw just one type of UML diagram. 

Keep in mind the following when evaluating diagramming tools.
* how you prefer to draw UML diagrams - text input or drawing
* who you need to collaborate with
* if you or your colleagues prefer to work in dark mode
* where you want to store your diagrams and related documentation
* confidentiality and data security
* output and publication formats
* other types of diagrams you need to draw

**Note:** Whichever application you choose, it should be able to save your diagrams in a format that can be opened by other applications. SVG is the most widely supported diagramming format. 

## Useful diagramming features for UML

A good UML diagramming tool should also have the following features to enable you to draw the full range of UML diagrams quickly and easily.

### Up-to-date UML shape libraries

To be able to draw all the [different types of UML diagrams](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/uml/), you'll need a wide variety of shapes that are kept up-to-date with the [UML specification](https://www.omg.org/spec/UML/2.5.1/About-UML/). 

Click _More Shapes_ at the bottom of the shape panel and enable both the [_UML 2.5_ and _UML_ shape libraries](https://www.drawio.com/blog/uml-2-5) in _Software_ section. 

draw.io includes 220 UML shapes for all types of UML diagrams, and many thousands of IT, general and cloud platform shapes for all types of technical diagrams. All these shape libraries are regularly updated and expanded.

[Image: The shapes in the UML and UML 2.5 shape library let you create all types of UML diagrams]

To diagram faster - [search for a shape's name](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/editor/panels/search-omnibox) to find it quickly. Add commonly used shapes and groups of shapes to the [scratchpad](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/editor/panels/scratchpad).

[Image: Search for shapes by their UML names to find them quickly]

### UML line styles - ends and labels 

[UML class diagrams](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/uml/class-diagrams) in particular need a large variety of arrow 'shapes' ([connector end styles](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/styles/connector-styles)) to indicate the associations between components of your system: inheritance (generalisation), aggregation, composition, and multiplicity. 

Use the connector end drop down lists in the _Style_ tab of the format panel to show the association type. 

[Image: Style your connector using the options in the Style tab in the format panel on the right in draw.io]

Again, UML class diagrams can require a lot of information to be attached to the connectors. [Labels](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/text/labels-add) can go in the centre (usage), or at either end (aggregation/composition). 

Double click on a connector in your draw.io diagram to add a label. Connectors can have multiple labels which will move with the connector as you reposition their attached class shapes. 

[Image: Symbols before the attribute and method names indicate visibility in UML class diagrams]

### Multi-page UML diagrams

When you need to draw an overview and separate diagrams for sub-processes or sub-systems, store them all in one diagram file. Add links on shapes in the higher-level diagram to navigate to the more detailed sub-systems on other diagram pages in draw.io. 

For example, the following collection of [UML state machine diagrams](https://www.drawio.com/docs/diagram-types/uml/state-diagrams) for a smart lock system are kept together in one four-page diagram. 

[[Image: An example top-level UML state machine diagram of a smart lock]](https://viewer.diagrams.net/?lightbox=1&highlight=0000ff&edit=_blank&layers=1&page=0&nav=1&title=#Uhttps%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2Fjgraph%2Fdrawio-diagrams%2Fdev%2Fblog%2Fuml-state-diagram-smart-lock.drawio)

[_Open this example in our diagram viewer_](https://viewer.diagrams.net/?lightbox=1&highlight=0000ff&edit=_blank&layers=1&page=0&nav=1&title=#Uhttps%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2Fjgraph%2Fdrawio-diagrams%2Fdev%2Fblog%2Fuml-state-diagram-smart-lock.drawio)

### UML templates

While UML diagram templates are good examples of how the many different UML diagram types should look, they aren't as useful as you might think. Your software, systems and processes are specific to your company and situation - you'll have to completely modify them or draw a diagram from scratch. 

Click _Arrange > Insert > Template_ and look in the _Software_ and _UML_ categories for UML diagram templates. 

[Image: Insert an UML activity diagram template in draw.io from the template library]

See the [draw.io diagram repository on GitHub](https://github.com/jgraph/drawio-diagrams/tree/dev/blog) for more examples. Alternatively, try the [generating diagrams in draw.io](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/generate/) to generate sequence, class and state diagrams. 

[Image: Generate a UML sequence diagram from a text description via the template library in draw.io] 

### Mermaid text input

[Mermaid](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/mermaid/) is a popular text-based UML diagramming tools and supported by draw.io. Many developers find describing sequence diagrams in particular easier using text.

Click _Arrange > Insert > Mermaid_. 

For example, the following Mermaid text generates a sequence diagram.
```
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    Student->>Admin: Can I enrol this semester?
    loop enrolmentCheck
        Admin->>Admin: Check previous results
    end
    Note right of Admin: Exam results may <br /> be delayed
    Admin-->>Student: Enrolment success
    Admin->>Professor: Assign student to tutor
    Professor-->>Admin: Student is assigned
```
[[Image: A simple sequence diagram inserted using the Mermaid syntax]](https://app.diagrams.net/?lightbox=1&highlight=0000ff&edit=_blank&layers=1&nav=1&page=3&title=#Uhttps%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2Fjgraph%2Fdrawio-diagrams%2Fmaster%2Fblog%2Fmermaid-examples.drawio)

Mermaid diagrams will use the built-in shapes by default so you can style and add to them using draw.io's tools afterwards.  

### AI diagram generation

The [diagram generation tool](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/generate/) in draw.io can draw some types of UML diagrams from text descriptions. Keep in mind that it does not know anything about your existing system, so it won't be able to draw an accurate class diagram, for example. 

Learn [when it makes sense to generate a diagram](https://www.drawio.com/docs/best-practice/generated-diagrams) and how to [write good queries](https://www.drawio.com/docs/best-practice/write-query-generate-diagram).
